title: Causative and reciprocal
intro: This unit adds two more voices to the verb, and a way to make verbs from nouns and adjectives. The causative is for making someone do something, or having it done: *gülmek* (to laugh) → *güldürmek* (to make laugh); *Saçymy kesdirdim* (I had my hair cut). The reciprocal is for what people do to each other or with each other: *görüşmek* (to meet), *düşünişmek* (to understand each other). And four suffixes turn nouns and adjectives into verbs: *az* (little) → *azalmak* (to decrease), *dost* (friend) → *dostlaşmak* (to make friends).

blocks.text: A causative verb brings in someone who makes, lets or has the action happen. *Çaga güldi*: the child laughed. *Men çagany güldürdim*: I made the child laugh. The new stem is a verb like any other, with every tense you know: *güldürýär*, *güldürdi*, *güldürer*, *güldürip*.

The causative suffix has several shapes. Two are regular enough to rely on: `-dYr` after a consonant, and *-t* after a vowel. *-t* also follows a stem of two or more syllables that ends in *l* or *r*, such as *bejer-* (repair) and the *-al*, *-el* verbs of the last section.

The vowel of `-dYr` follows harmony and the rounding rule, as in any suffix: *kesdir-*, *güldür-*, *ýuwdur-*, *aldyr-*. The *-t* is a soft one: like the *t* of *gitmek* ([A1 unit 6](a1-u06)), it turns into *d* before a vowel and before *-ýar*, *-ýär*, and stays *t* before a consonant.
Other verbs have a causative of their own shape, with *-yr*, *-ar*, *-uz* or a new stem. You have met several of them as words. Learn each one with its verb:

blocks.caption: Causatives to learn as words
head: Verb
Causative
Meaning
rows: to put to bed; to lay down
to wake (someone) up, to get (someone) up
to take out, to take off

blocks.text: *Getirmek*, to bring, is literally **to make come**. For **to make go**, **to take away**, Turkmen uses *äkitmek*: *Çagany mekdebe äkitdim*, I took the child to school; *Bu stakany äkit*, take this glass away.

items.en: This film made me laugh.
My mum woke me up at seven.
Aýna teaches English at school.
Sorry, I kept you waiting.
I stopped a taxi.
I took the book back to the library.

blocks.title: Soft t: okadýar, but okatdy
blocks.text: The *-t* of the causative turns into *d* before a vowel and before *-ýar*: *okadýar*, *okadyp*, *azaldýar*. Before a consonant it stays *t*: *okatdy*, *okatjak*, *okatmaly*, *okatmaýar*. Not `okatýar`, and not `okaddy`.

blocks.title: Two ways to teach
blocks.text: *Öwretmek* is to teach someone something: *Ol maňa küşt oýnamagy öwretdi*, he taught me to play chess. *Okatmak*, literally **to make read**, is to teach a subject or at a school: *Ol mekdepde taryh okadýar*, she teaches history at a school.

sections.title: Who does what: the person you make act

blocks.text: A causative sentence has two doers: the one who makes it happen, the subject, and the one who does the action. Where the second one goes depends on the verb you started from.

If that verb has no object of its own (*gülmek* to laugh, *aglamak* to cry, *ýatmak* to lie down, *turmak* to get up), the person made to act becomes the object, in the accusative: *Çaga güldi* → *Men çagany güldürdim*. *Bäbek ýatdy* → *Ejesi bäbegi ýatyrdy*, the mother put the baby to bed.

If the verb already has an object (*almak* to buy, *geýmek* to put on, *içmek* to drink, *ýuwmak* to wash), that object keeps the accusative, and the person made to act goes in the dative: *Kakam kitap aldy* → *Men kakama kitap aldyrdym*, I had my dad buy a book. *Gyzy täze köýnek geýdi* → *Ejesi gyzyna täze köýnek geýdirdi*, her mother put a new dress on her.

blocks.caption: Where the person made to act goes
head: Starting verb
Person made to act
Example
rows: *Çagany güldürdim.* I made the child laugh.
*Kakama kitap aldyrdym.* I had my dad buy a book.

blocks.text: Very often the person who does the work isn't named at all, and English says **have something done** or **get something done**. This is how you talk about services and errands: *Saçymy kesdirdim* (I had my hair cut), *Köýnegimi ýuwdurdym* (I had my shirt washed), *Maşynymy bejertdim* (I had my car repaired), *Surat çekdirdim* (I had my photo taken).

items.en: I had my hair cut yesterday.
She had a new dress made.
I had my dad buy a book.
The mother gave the baby some milk.
This book made me cry.
The teacher had us write the new words.

blocks.title: Kakama, not kakamy
blocks.text: With a verb that already has an object, the accusative is taken by the thing: *kitaby*, *köýnegi*. The person you get to do it goes in the dative: *Kitaby kakama aldyrdym*, I had my dad buy the book. The same goes for *ýatlatmak*, to remind: *Maňa ýatlat!*, remind me!

blocks.title: Saç aldyrmak
blocks.text: For a haircut you will also hear *saç aldyrmak*, literally **to have the hair taken**. This course uses *saçymy kesdirdim*; both are understood.

The reciprocal `-(Y)ş`, just *-ş* after a vowel, is for what two or more people do to each other or with each other. You already know several reciprocal verbs as words: *görüşmek* (to meet, to see each other), *gürleşmek* (to talk, to chat), *tanyşmak* (to get to know each other), *salamlaşmak* (to greet each other) and *hoşlaşmak* (to say goodbye).

blocks.caption: Reciprocal verbs
head: Verb
Reciprocal
Meaning
rows: to meet, to see each other
to get to know each other (a new stem)

blocks.text: The subject is plural, or one person with *bilen* (with) and the other: *Biz görüşdik* (we met), *Men Aýna bilen görüşdim* (I met Aýna, literally I met with Aýna). The suffix itself says **each other**: *Olar gowy düşünişýärler*, they understand each other well.

When a verb has no reciprocal form, or you need **each other** with a case, use *biri-biri* in the case the verb takes: *biri-birine* (to each other), *biri-birini* (each other, as an object), *biri-biri bilen* (with each other), *biri-birinden* (from each other). For **we** and **you** it takes the possessive: *biri-birimize* (to each other, of us), *biri-biriňize* (of you). In writing you will also meet *birek-birege*, **to each other**.

items.en: We meet every week.
I talked with Merdan on the phone.
They understand each other well.
They help each other.
We write to each other.
They have known each other for a long time.

blocks.title: The case of the verb
blocks.text: *Biri-biri* takes the case the verb needs. *Kömek etmek* takes the dative, so *biri-birine kömek etmek*; *tanamak* takes the accusative, so *biri-birini tanamak*. And with a reciprocal verb you don't need it at all: *Biz görüşdik*, not `biz biri-birimiz bilen görüşdik`.

blocks.title: Tanyşdyrmak: both at once
blocks.text: A reciprocal can take the causative: *tanyşmak* (to get to know each other) → *tanyşdyrmak* (to introduce, literally to make get to know each other): *Ol meni ejesi bilen tanyşdyrdy*, she introduced me to her mother.

Turkmen makes many verbs from nouns and adjectives with four suffixes. You have met a good number of these verbs as words; here is how they are built. Not every noun takes every suffix, so learn the verbs as words, but the pattern helps you guess what a new one means.

blocks.caption: Four suffixes that make verbs
head: Suffix
Meaning
Examples
rows: do something with it; make it so
*kyn* → *kynlaşmak* (to get harder); *ýakyn* → *ýakynlaşmak* (to come closer); *dost* → *dostlaşmak* (to make friends)
*gahar* → *gaharlanmak* (to get angry); *alada* → *aladalanmak* (to worry); *öý* → *öýlenmek* (to marry, of a man)

blocks.text: `-Al` after a vowel: after *a* or *e* it is just *-l*, *gysga* (short) → *gysgalmak* (to get shorter); a final *y* or *i* drops, *uly* → *ulalmak* (to grow up), *kiçi* → *kiçelmek* (to get smaller).

These verbs often take a causative in turn, with *-t* after the *l*: *azalmak* → *azaltmak* (to reduce), *köpelmek* → *köpeltmek* (to make more), *ulalmak* → *ulaltmak* (to bring up, to raise). After *n* it is `-dYr`: *gaharlanmak* → *gaharlandyrmak* (to make angry).

items.en: We became friends at school.
The exam is getting closer.
When autumn comes, the days get shorter.
He grew up in a village.
Prices went down.
I forgot to salt the soup.

blocks.title: -laş is not always each other
blocks.text: *Dostlaşmak* (to make friends) and *kömekleşmek* (to help each other) are done together, but *kynlaşmak* and *ýakynlaşmak* only mean **to get harder** and **to come closer**. Let the noun or adjective guide you.

lines.en: Are you ready for the wedding?

lines.tk: Entek däl. Täze köýnek tikdirdim, ýöne ony entek almadym.
lines.en: Not yet. I've had a new dress made, but I haven't picked it up yet.
Where are you going to get your hair cut?

lines.tk: Aýgül daýzada. Ol meni hiç haçan garaşdyrmaýar.
lines.en: At Aýgül daýza's. She never keeps me waiting.
How did Kerim and Bahar meet?

lines.tk: Olary bir dostlary tanyşdyrdy. Soň olar her gün telefonda gürleşip başladylar.
lines.en: A friend of theirs introduced them. Then they started talking on the phone every day.
And now the wedding is getting close!

lines.tk: Hawa. Myhmanlar hem köpeldi: üç ýüz adam gelýär!
lines.en: Yes. And the guest list has grown: three hundred people are coming!

summary: The causative is `-dYr` after a consonant (*kesdir-, güldür-*), *-t* after a vowel and after *l* or *r* in a stem of two or more syllables (*okat-, azalt-, bejert-*); other verbs have their own shape (*turuz-, içir-, görkez-, getir-*).
The causative *-t* turns into *d* before a vowel and *-ýar*: *okadýar*, but *okatdy*.
With a verb that has no object, the person made to act takes the accusative: *Çagany güldürdim*.
With a verb that has an object, the person takes the dative: *Kakama kitap aldyrdym*. With no person named, it is **have it done**: *Saçymy kesdirdim*.
The reciprocal `-(Y)ş` says **each other** or **together**: *görüşmek, gürleşmek, düşünişmek*.
*Biri-biri* takes the case of the verb: *biri-birine kömek etmek*, *biri-birini tanamak*; *biri-birimize* for **we**.
`-lA`, `-lAş`, `-lAn` and `-Al` make verbs from words: *duzlamak, dostlaşmak, gaharlanmak, azalmak*.
